newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian Metals - Buying steady, trade awaits Chinese.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals - Buying steady, trade awaits Chinese.

text.p: Base metals demand in Asia has picked up steam after the long Lunar New Year and Hari Raya holidays and the trade is on the lookout for signs of renewed Chinese buying, Singapore base metal dealers said on Friday.

"There is a belief that this is the period the Chinese will come back into the market," the general manager of a European metal trading company told Reuters. "The Chinese have been making some inquiries."

Another trader with a foreign metal brokerage house said he is beginning to see signs that Chinese buyers "are starting to come in slowly. They may step up buying after the funeral of Deng next week."
The trader was refering to the six-day mourning period declared by Beijing to honour the memory of Chinese paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, who died at age 92 on Wednesday.
But another dealer said he believed Chinese buyers, needing prompt delivery of metal, would not wait for the end of the mourning period.
"Life goes on. Business goes on," he said.
The only likely deterrent to Chinese buying would be the current high prices of base metals like copper on the London Metal Exchange (LME).

Three month copper prices were quoted in London late on Thursday at US$2,236/40 a tonne. Copper was quoted in Singapore at $2,235/40 a tonne at 0245 GMT on Friday. Cash copper was seen at $2,414/19 a tonne with the backwardation pegged at $79.
"The Chinese are taking stock of the situation. If they need the metal for immediate delivery, I don't think the steep price will put them off," one trader said.
"I think copper is due to come off in the LME. That may encourage the Chinese to take some metal," one dealer said.
The base metal business in Asia remains buoyant with the can industry in Japan expected to increase its consumption of aluminium in the second quarter of the year, traders said.
"The can industries in Japan are now very busy," a Japanese trader said, adding their demand for the metal in the second quarter should rise by at least 20 percent over the same period last year.
"Business around the region is okay, but not exceedingly good," another trader said.
Premiums, reflecting the healthy demand around the region, were steady to slightly higher, traders said.
Copper premiums for Grade A cathodes were seen between $20-$40 a tonne, against $20-$30 the previous week, while Western aluminium ingots were reported steady at about $65-$85.
"Demand right now is really mostly steady, but there's no major buying going on at the moment," a senior dealer for a Japanese metal trading firm said.
The base metal trade is also looking at whether several thousand tonnes of Chinese copper which arrived in Singapore earlier this week will be placed on warrant at the LME warehouse here.

"I think 5,000 tonnes is a reasonable figure," the general manager of a European metal trading firm said when asked for an estimate on the amount of Chinese copper shipped to Singapore. "But it's a question how much of that material will make it to warrant here."
The volume of copper in the LME's Singapore warehouse fell slightly to 54,050 tonnes in the stock report on Tuesday, down 400 tonnes from the previous LME stocks report released last Friday.
